newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Viet repatriations bring boatpeople epic end nearer.
newsitem.headline: Viet repatriations bring boatpeople epic end nearer.

text.p: Hong Kong bundled 245 "boatpeople" back to Vietnam on Wednesday in the last major repatriation of "voluntary returnees", a key milestone in efforts to end a 20-year saga of refugee anguish.
Hong Kong authorities also pressed ahead with a drive to rid the territory of die-hard asylum seekers who have refused to go home despite failing to prove they are genuine refugees.
The Hong Kong office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) sent 245 voluntary returnees to Vietnam on two chartered planes and one commercial flight on Wednesday.
"These are the last chartered flights for voluntary returns," UNHCR official Preeta Law told Reuters.

"Although the UNHCR will continue to facilitate the return of volunteers to Vietnam, the voluntary repatriation programme is coming to a close and no further voluntary repatriation flights will be scheduled," she said.
The UNHCR office said 57,363 Vietnamese boatpeople had been returned to Vietnam voluntarily under UNHCR auspices since 1989.

The Hong Kong government said that this Friday it will also send back 181 who are considered to be merely economic migrants and not real refugees, under a forced repatriation scheme which has already sent home 10,367 failed asylum seekers since 1991.
The efforts mark a final push to rid Hong Kong refugee camps of Vietnamese boatpeople before China takes Hong Kong back from Britain on July 1. Beijing insists they be gone by that time.
One of the obstacles that has slowed the flow until now has been Vietnam's failure to approve a large number of the migrants for repatriation from Hong Kong.

The United States, Britain, Sweden and France agreed this week to accept dozens of the Vietnamese refugees, a step forward but still a long way from resettling the 1,382 Vietnamese here who are recognised as refugees but have no offers of a home.
Hong Kong camps also contain 1,465 "non-refugees" who are considered illegal immigrants. a government official said.

The boatpeople are the last of a floodtide of tens of thousands who have fled to Southeast Asian territories, many on flimsy boats, since the communists won the Vietnam War in 1975. As the drama nears an end in Hong Kong, there have been poignant reminders in recent days of how thin the line may be between a refugee and an illegal migrant.

A Vietnamese government accountant who was forced to clean out pigsties back home because of his political views won a court battle and succeeded this week in a last-ditch attempt to avoid being sent home.
And a father of eight who fled Vietnam after being accused of spying for the United States won refugee status for his family just days before they were due to be repatriated.
Frustrated by grim living conditions and years -- in some cases more than a decade -- of confinement, some Vietnamese boatpeople have turned to violence in the camps in recent years.

Last June inmates set fire to a Hong Kong detention camp and staged a mas breakout but were quickly rounded up. Breakout attempts on a smaller scale are continuing. And some inmates commit crimnes or try to wound themselves to delay departure.
Hong Kong legislators have urged the government to ask Britain to take in all Vietnamese who remain in the territory at the time of its handover to China.
